Bara
bah-RAH
v. (Hebrew)
Hebrew bārā’, “to create.” In the Old Testament, used exclusively of God’s creative activity; never used of human making. The grammatical subject of bārā’ in its biblical uses is always God.

Biblical Definition

Bārā’ is the great Hebrew creation-verb—the word with which the Bible opens (in the beginning God created (bārā’) the heaven and the earth, Gen 1:1) and the word that is used uniformly across the Old Testament for God’s creative activity. Two grammatical features mark the verb as theologically distinctive. First, its grammatical subject is always God: bārā’ is not used of human creative making (for which other verbs are used: ‘āsāh, to make; yātsar, to form, as a potter forms clay); it is reserved for the activity that only God performs. Second, it does not require pre-existing material: while the verb can in some contexts describe creative ordering of existing material (as ‘āsāh typically does), in its supreme uses (Gen 1:1; Isa 40:26; Isa 45:7, 12, 18) it carries the sense of creation out of nothing—the bringing into being of what previously had no existence. The doctrine of creatio ex nihilo (creation out of nothing) is therefore grounded in the biblical use of bārā’. The verb appears at several theologically weighty hinges across the Old Testament. The creation of the heavens and the earth: in the beginning God created the heaven and the earth (Gen 1:1). The creation of man in the image of God: so God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them (Gen 1:27—three uses of bārā’ in one verse). The creation of new heavens and a new earth in eschatological promise: for, behold, I create new heavens and a new earth: and the former shall not be remembered, nor come into mind (Isa 65:17). The pastoral promise of a renewed inward life: create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me (Ps 51:10—David asking God to perform the very work only God can perform, on his sin-broken inner life). The verb’s structural use therefore traces an arc: God created in the beginning, God created man in His image, God will create new heavens and earth at the end, and God creates a clean heart in the redeemed sinner now. The verb in each case names the activity that only God performs, that requires no pre-existing material in its supreme uses, and that grounds the entire biblical doctrine of God as Creator distinct from and sovereign over all His creatures.

Webster 1828 Definition

(Hebrew term.) Bārā’: to create; the great OT creation-verb whose grammatical subject is always God; foundation of the doctrine of creatio ex nihilo and of the biblical distinction between Creator and creature.

CREATE, v.t. — To produce; to bring into being from nothing; to cause to exist. In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth (Gen 1:1). 2. To produce, as a work of imagination. 3. To form anew; to change the state or condition. Create in me a clean heart, O God (Ps 51:10).

BARA — (Hebrew verb, H1254.) To create. Grammatical subject always God in OT usage; 54 OT occurrences. The great verb of creatio ex nihilo.

Key Scripture

Genesis 1:1 — "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth."

Genesis 1:27 — "So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them."

Psalm 51:10 — "Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me."

Isaiah 65:17 — "For, behold, I create new heavens and a new earth: and the former shall not be remembered, nor come into mind."

Modern Corruption

Bārā’-shaped doctrine of creation is corrupted, in the contemporary cultural landscape, by the naturalistic-evolutionary account that has displaced the biblical Creator with impersonal processes—and by the inverse error of the theistic-evolution synthesis that has retained the word create while emptying it of the direct-divine-causation the Hebrew verb carries.

expand to see more

Naturalistic-evolutionary accounts of cosmic and biological origins have, across the past century and a half, displaced the biblical Creator with impersonal processes—quantum fluctuations producing the cosmos from nothing-via-physical-laws (which are themselves not nothing), Darwinian natural selection producing biological complexity from simpler ancestors via unguided mutation and selection, the long sweep of cosmic history understood as the playing-out of physical processes without divine involvement. The biblical doctrine of bārā’ refuses this. Creation is the personal act of God—the heaven and the earth, the man in His image, the new heavens and new earth, the clean heart in the redeemed sinner—and the verb’s grammatical subject is always God. The recovery is not chiefly scientific (the church has variously engaged the scientific questions and ought to continue) but doctrinal: the affirmation that God created, that He alone is Creator, that the cosmos is His artifact and not an unguided process, that He continues to create (the new heart, the new heavens and earth) in His sovereign activity across history and into eternity.

The opposite corruption is the theistic-evolution synthesis that has retained the word create while emptying it of the direct-divine-causation the Hebrew verb carries. On this account, God created by means of the evolutionary process; He set the process in motion at the beginning and superintended it providentially; the biblical creation accounts are taken as theological poetry compatible with the scientific narrative of long evolutionary development. The Christian tradition has variously assessed this synthesis, and the question of how God created remains contested across faithful Christians. But the integrity of the doctrine of creation requires preserving what bārā’ grammatically carries: the direct activity of God, the personal causation, the bringing into being of what would not otherwise exist—not merely the providential superintendence of impersonal processes. Recover both ends. Refuse the naturalistic displacement of the Creator, and preserve in any theistic-evolutionary synthesis the substantive direct-divine-causation the biblical verb carries. The God who created the heavens and the earth, who created man in His image, who will create new heavens and earth, and who creates a clean heart in the redeemed sinner is the personal Creator the biblical verb names—and any account of origins, ours or scientific, must preserve the substance of the verb if it would not lose the doctrine.

Hebrew Roots

Hebrew bārā’ (to create); grammatical subject always God; the great verb of creatio ex nihilo; structurally tracing the arc from creation in the beginning, through man’s creation in God’s image, to the new heavens and earth and the clean heart God creates in the redeemed sinner.

expand to see more

Hebrew bārā’ (H1254) — to create (54 OT uses; grammatical subject always God).

Hebrew ‘āsāh (H6213) — to make, do (cousin verb, used of both God and man; often paralleled with bārā’).

Hebrew yātsar (H3335) — to form (as a potter forms clay; used of God’s forming of man in Gen 2:7).

Greek ktizō (G2936) — to create (the NT counterpart; Eph 2:10; 3:9; Col 1:16; 3:10; Rev 4:11).

Usage

"In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth—the Bible opens with bārā’ and the doctrine of creation."

"The grammatical subject of bārā’ is always God in OT usage—the verb is reserved for activity only God performs."

"Naturalistic-evolutionary accounts displace the Creator with processes; theistic-evolution synthesis empties the verb of direct-divine-causation; biblical bārā’ names the personal creative activity of God across the arc of redemptive history."
